title: Home life
hookLine: he mended his own sandals, patched his clothes, and helped at home (Bukhari)

lines: WHAT DID HE DO AT HOME?
cards: Battles, treaties, sieges, revelations: for days now, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ has been in big moments. It's easy to imagine a man who only ever stood in front of crowds.
So somebody once asked Aisha the most ordinary question about him. What did he do at home? Not in the mosque, not on the battlefield.
At home, with the door shut, when nobody important was watching. People can be quite different in their own kitchens. Her answer is short, and Sahih al-Bukhari keeps it.

teach.b: Aisha says: he used to be busy serving his family, and when the time for prayer came, he went out to pray. The leader of a whole community, at home, helping. Other reports fill in the picture.
Asked again, she said he mended his own sandals, patched his own clothes, milked his goat, and did the kinds of work men do in their homes. He served himself. And home was simple.
His rooms were small, built against the wall of the mosque, with ceilings low enough to touch. His bed, Bukhari says, was leather stuffed with palm fiber.

teach.h: A MAT THAT MARKED HIS SIDE.
teach.b: Once Umar came in, saw the marks the rough mat had pressed into the Prophet's side, and wept, thinking of the emperors of Persia and Rome in their luxury.

The Prophet answered gently: wouldn't you be content that they have this world, and we have the next? Aisha also remembered months when no fire was lit in their houses for cooking: they lived on dates and water.
None of this was a show.
And he put it into words in a hadith in at-Tirmidhi: the best of you are the best to their families, and I am the best of you to my family.
Teachers often draw a quiet standard from it: whatever someone is in public, the measure is taken at home, with the sandals and the patches and the dishes.

how: Muslim teachers often hold up the Prophet's home life as a model for husbands and fathers sharing housework, often quoting Aisha's answer and the hadith that the best of you are the best to their families.

o: the years the Prophet spent at home before revelation
the rules of a Muslim household set out in the Qur'an
how the Prophet lived and served his family at home

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: he was busy serving his family
wept at the marks of the mat

s: the Prophet had servants mend his clothes
Aisha said he mended his sandals and patched his clothes himself.
when prayer time came, he left the housework and went to pray
busy serving his family, and when the prayer came, he went out.
the hadith says the best of you are the best to their families
and, he added, I am the best of you to my family.

games.q: Umar walks in and sees the rough mat's marks on the Prophet's side. he starts to cry, thinking of kings on silk. what does the Prophet say?
o: you're right, bring me a better bed.
wouldn't you be content: they have this world, we the next?
games.why: he asked if Umar wouldn't be content that they have this world, and we have the next. the mat stayed.

practice: Picture the task at home you always leave for someone else, or for later: the shoes by the door, the button that fell off, the dishes, the trash nobody wants to take out.
Pick one and picture yourself doing it carefully, as if it matters, because in this story it does. If you live alone, pick the one you avoid the most.

wordCard.voice: Home life. The Prophet at home: serving his family, mending his own sandals and clothes, and living simply. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: in the service of his family, Aisha's words in Bukhari 676.

carryVoice: Your line: he mended his own shoes. Sandals, patches, a goat to milk. That's day two hundred seventy.
